meta.title: Old English Alphabet and Pronunciation
meta.subtitle: 41 letters, sounds and spelling rules · both directions, as two cards per note
meta.desc: How to read Old English: 41 notes, the first deck of the Old English collection. Both directions: see a letter and recall its sound, or see a sound and recall the letter, each a card with its own schedule. The vowels short and long — a macron (ā, ē, ī) marks a long one, an editor's mark the manuscripts do not have — then the diphthongs (ea, eo, ie), the consonants that are not said as in modern English (c always k, ċ ch, ġ y, sċ sh, h like the ch of 'loch' after a vowel, f s and þ voiced between vowels), the rules that hold for every word (every letter is said, a double consonant is held long, the prefix ġe- is never stressed), the letters said as today, and three letters a reader of the manuscripts meets: wynn (ƿ), the insular g and the abbreviation ꝥ for þæt. Each note describes the sound in English words with the IPA in brackets — the same IPA the level decks print under every headword — and gives one or two words from those decks that show it. There is no speaker, because no voice reads Old English; the sounds are the standard scholarly reconstruction of late West Saxon, the literary language of about the year 1000. Sources: H. Sweet, An Anglo-Saxon Primer, 8th ed. (1905), 'Sounds' (public domain); the example words and their pronunciations are English Wiktionary's, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0).

fields.Name: short a
fields.Sound: a short a, between the a of "cat" and the a of "father" [ɑ]
fields.Example: habban[ˈhɑb.bɑn]to have, possess

fields.Name: long a
fields.Sound: the a of "father", held long [ɑː]

fields.Name: ash (æsc)
fields.Sound: the a of "cat" [æ]
fields.Example: dæġ/dæj/day, (usually) as a period from sunrise to sunset and (scientifically) as a 24-hour period from sunrise to sunrise

fields.Name: long ash
fields.Sound: the a of "cat", held long [æː]

fields.Name: short e
fields.Sound: the e of "bet" [e]

fields.Name: long e
fields.Sound: a long, pure e, like German "See" — without the glide of English "day" [eː]

fields.Name: short i
fields.Sound: the i of "sit" [i]

fields.Name: long i
fields.Sound: the ee of "feet" [iː]

fields.Name: short o
fields.Sound: a short o, as in British "hot" but with rounder lips [o]

fields.Name: long o
fields.Sound: a long, pure o, like German "so" — without the glide of English "go" [oː]

fields.Name: short u
fields.Sound: the u of "put" [u]

fields.Name: long u
fields.Sound: the oo of "moon" [uː]

fields.Name: short y
fields.Sound: the i of "sit" said with rounded lips, like German ü or French u [y]

fields.Name: long y
fields.Sound: the ee of "feet" said with rounded lips and held, like German "kühn" [yː]

fields.Name: short diphthong
fields.Sound: æ gliding into a, in one syllable [æ͜ɑ]

fields.Name: long diphthong
fields.Sound: æ gliding into a, held long [æ͜ɑː]

fields.Name: short diphthong
fields.Sound: e gliding into o, in one syllable [e͜o]

fields.Name: long diphthong
fields.Sound: e gliding into o, held long [e͜oː]

fields.Name: short diphthong (early West Saxon)
fields.Sound: i gliding into y, in one syllable; later scribes write i or y for it [i͜y]

fields.Name: long diphthong (early West Saxon)
fields.Sound: i gliding into y, held long; later scribes write ī or ȳ for it [i͜yː]

fields.Name: c without a dot
fields.Sound: always k, as in "king" — never s [k]
fields.Example:
cuman/ˈku.mɑn/to come
cyning[ˈky.niŋɡ]king

fields.Name: c with a dot
fields.Sound: ch, as in "church" — the dot is an editor's, the manuscripts write c [t͡ʃ]
fields.Example:
ċild[t͡ʃiɫd]child
iċ/it͡ʃ/I

fields.Name: g without a dot
fields.Sound: g as in "go"; between back vowels a softer, rubbed g, like Dutch g [ɡ], [ɣ]

fields.Name: g with a dot
fields.Sound: y, as in "yes" — the dot is an editor's, the manuscripts write g [j]
fields.Example:
ġēar/jæ͜ɑːr/year
dæġ/dæj/day, (usually) as a period from sunrise to sunset and (scientifically) as a 24-hour period from sunrise to sunrise

fields.Name: cg
fields.Sound: dg, as in "edge", held long; the manuscripts write cg [dd͡ʒ]
fields.Example: seċġan[ˈsed.d͡ʒɑn]to say, tell

fields.Name: sc
fields.Sound: sh, as in "ship"; the manuscripts write sc [ʃ]
fields.Example:
sċip/ʃip/ship
sċēap/ʃæ͜ɑːp/sheep

fields.Name: h
fields.Sound: h as in "house" at the start of a word; after a vowel, the ch of Scottish "loch" or German "ich" [h], [x], [ç]
fields.Example:
hund[hund]dog
niht[niçt]night

fields.Name: h before a consonant
fields.Sound: a breathed, voiceless w, l, n or r: hw like the wh of Scottish "which", hl an l said with a puff of breath [ʍ], [l̥]
fields.Example:
hwæt[ʍæt]what
hlāf[l̥ɑːf]bread

fields.Name: f
fields.Sound: f as in "fit"; between voiced sounds, v as in "over" [f], [v]
fields.Example:
fæder/ˈfæ.der/father
heofon[ˈhe͜o.von]sky

fields.Name: s
fields.Sound: s as in "sit"; between voiced sounds, z as in "rise" [s], [z]
fields.Example:
sāwol/ˈsɑː.wol/soul
rīsan[ˈriː.zɑn]to rise

fields.Name: thorn and eth
fields.Sound: th as in "thin"; between voiced sounds, th as in "this". The two letters are ONE sound, and scribes use either [θ], [ð]
fields.Example:
þing[θiŋɡ]thing
ōþer[ˈoː.ðer]other

fields.Name: r
fields.Sound: a trilled or tapped r, always said, after a vowel too [r]
fields.Example:
rīċe/ˈriː.t͡ʃe/kingdom, empire
heorte[ˈhe͜orˠ.te]heart

fields.Name: x
fields.Sound: ks, as in "axe" [ks]

fields.Name: n before g
fields.Sound: ng with the g sounded, as in "finger", never as in "singer" [ŋɡ]
fields.Example:
singan[ˈsiŋ.ɡɑn]to sing, chant
cyning[ˈky.niŋɡ]king

fields.Name: two consonants at the start
fields.Sound: every letter is said — no silent letters: the k of cniht, the w of wrītan [kn], [wr]
fields.Example:
cniht[kniçt]boy
āwrītanto write

fields.Name: double consonants
fields.Sound: a double consonant is held long, as in Italian or in "bookcase": hab-ban, sit-tan [bː], [tː]
fields.Example:
habban[ˈhɑb.bɑn]to have, possess
sittan/ˈsit.tɑn/to sit

fields.Name: an unstressed prefix
fields.Sound: said lightly, "yeh": a word is stressed on its first syllable, but never on ġe-, be- or for- [je]
fields.Example:
ġesēon/jeˈse͜oːn/to see
forġiefan[forˈji͜y.vɑn]to forgive, to give

fields.Letter: b, d, l, m, n, p, t, w
fields.Name: the rest
fields.Sound: as in modern English: b, d, l, m, n, p, t, w [b], [d], [l], [m], [n], [p], [t], [w]
fields.Example:
mōdor/ˈmoː.dor/mother
wīf/wiːf/woman
fields.Word: b, d, l, m, n, p, t, w

fields.Name: wynn
fields.Sound: the manuscripts' letter for w, taken from a rune; editions print w

fields.Name: insular g (yogh)
fields.Sound: the manuscripts' shape of g, said g or y as above; editions print g

fields.Name: the abbreviation for þæt
fields.Sound: a crossed thorn: the scribes' shorthand for þæt "that", as & is for "and"
